angle: Ledgerline cuts write amplification by tracking garbage per key, and pays for it with an in-memory index and no range scans.

threads.post:
Ledgerline compacts one key at a time, so a hot key never forces a rewrite of cold segments.

Every write appends to a segment; an in-memory index points each key to its latest record.
On the README benchmark: write amplification 1.3 vs 7.5 for RocksDB, p99 writes at 0.4 ms.
The cost is RAM: about 48 bytes per key, and no efficient range scans.
threads.reply:
The baseline is RocksDB with default options. HN commenters point out that tuned universal compaction would close part of the gap, and that the design is close to Bitcask with finer garbage accounting.

Source: https://github.com/example/ledgerline

tiktok.title: A log store that compacts one key at a time
tiktok.description: Ledgerline appends every write and tracks garbage per key instead of per segment. Write amplification drops to 1.3 on its benchmark, but the whole index must fit in RAM. #databases #rust #storage

slides.heading: Compaction per key, not per segment
slides.body: Ledgerline is an embedded append-only log store in Rust.

slides.heading: How it works
bullets: Each write appends to the active segment file
An in-memory index maps a key to its latest offset
Superseded records are counted per key
Past compact_after, only that key's live record is rewritten

slides.label: write amplification, vs 7.5 for RocksDB
slides.body: README benchmark: one NVMe SSD, 16 threads, 1 KiB values, Zipfian keys. RocksDB ran with default options.

slides.heading: The API
slides.body: Plain key-value calls. No transactions across keys.

slides.heading: What it costs
right: About 48 bytes of RAM per key

slides.heading: Verdict
slides.body: A strong fit for write-heavy key-value data that fits in memory. Benchmark it against a tuned RocksDB before switching.
right: You need range scans or time series
Billions of keys on one node
